div.head: Software architecture plays a central role in large, complex software systems with real-time or safety-critical requirements. We are investigating design methods based on software architecture, and techniques to specifi, represent, and analyze them. As a practical mattel; we have decided to focus our architectural research on sysrem structure, communication behavior and specijc non-functional properties such as pelformance, synchronization, architectural integrity, dependency analysis and control. Introduction
div.p: Software architecture plays a central role in many systems where the functionality of the product is provided by large, complex software systems with real-time or safetycritical requirements. We are investigating design methods based on software architecture, and techniques to specify, represent, and analyze them. Such methods need to assure non-functional system properties (such as performance), improve reliability and safety, and increase productivity.

To help us identify concrete issues related to design and analysis of large systems, we have conducted a survey of a variety of architectures [9]. We have selected a system from the instrumentation domain to demonstrate the usefulness of our design and analysis methods. The Instrumentation System collects data from a number of remote sensors and generates a variety of reports. Safety and real-time performance are some of the important system characteristics.

Engineers would like to assure that such products satisfy critical performance requirements, starting with the high-level design, and continuing through implementation. They would like to identify and eliminate performance bottlenecks in the architecture and ensure the predictability and analyzability of the architecture.

Real-time system design demands careful attention to temporal properties. There are explicit timing requirements on the tasks processed by the computer system. The most common requirement is that a task be completed within a certain time period, which is often referred to as a hard deadline. Failure to meet the deadline could result in the system failing.

The current practice is to use a combination of worstcase scenario experiments, engineering judgement, and empirical testing. Worst case scenarios are created and manually simulated to ensure that systems meet their realtime constraints. This has to be redone every time a change is requested. A tool that models this system behavior and supports tuning and analysis of system parameters would be very useful.

Many tools analyzing real-time applications focus on scheduling parameters, time constraints, specification of execution, resource policy, and verification [ 1,6]. However, it is hard for software engineers to model and implement the actual system because they have less information about the software architecture. In this paper, we show how software architecture can provide support for realtime analysis (such as RMA [ 5 ] ) during system design, and how the resulting analysis can also provide feedback to evaluate the design decisions made at the architecture level. high-level configuration or architectural language (e.g., MetaH [ 1 I]) we view the software architecture of a system from a variety of perspectives [8]. Each perspective deals with a particular set of concerns. For our purposes, we will focus on two of these perspectives, the conceptual and execution structures.

div.head: Conceptual and Execution Structures
div.p: The conceptual structure describes the system in terms of its major design elements and the relationships among them. This is a very high-level and domain-specific perspective of the system, using design elements and relationships specific to the application domain. It is how the product engineer would view the system in problem specific terms. Conceptual structures are used to enable the assignment and partitioning of system functionality, and to specify and analyze domain-specific system properties.

The basic elements of a real-time system include tasks, the file system, and a variety of communication and synchronization mechanisms such as event flags, mailboxes, messages queues, etc. The functionality of the conceptual structure must eventually be mapped to these elements to obtain the execution structure. This mapping requires a partitioning and assignment of system functionality. The decisions made during the mapping process are guided by concerns such as: functional cohesion, physical cohesion (locality), communication bandwidth required, characteristics of the communication traffic (sporadic vs. periodic, flow rate), and periodicity. Different trade-offs between these concerns will result in different execution structures.

The conceptual and execution structures are used by the product engineer for designing real-time systems and evaluating its performance. Different designs will be developed and evaluated based on different design factors such as work load requirements, task characteristics, performance criteria, and the software and hardware platform. Software architecture not only supports the designers in making the decisions to optimize the system performance but also provides a framework for product engineers to model and implement the actual system.

div.head: Analysis Approach
div.p: In our experimental study, we first defined and described selected performance and schedulability properties for the Instrumentation System. We developed an incremental model of the system, and then defined the information necessary to check the properties of interest in the software architecture. First we focused on the application-level model of the system. Then, we looked at the system platform and factored in the time for sending and receiving messages, the time for storing data to disk, and the overhead from the operating system. Finally, we considered alternative designs.

The various factors [2,7] that we considered in constructing a model are shown in Figure 1. We carried out the performance analysis using the following steps: Identify worst case workload. We characterized the worst case workload in terms of the number of remote sensors and the rates of the incoming signal data.

Identify critical performance requirements. We identified end-to-end execution paths for each external stimulus such as the arrival of signal data. An execution path is a sequence of actions executed in response to the external stimulus. The performance requirements for each path determines the deadline for the path.

div.p: Identify and model critical resources. We identified the critical resources in the hardware and software platforms and constructed a model. Make architectural design decisions. We looked at the heuristics used by the engineers to determine how software components are mapped to tasks, the priorities of such tasks, and the various buffer sizes.

div.head: Perform analysis and analyze results.
div.p: Given the design decisions and the analysis model, we carried out the performance analysis and evaluated the various design decisions.

div.head: Experimental Study
div.p: For the purpose of illustration, we will use a simplified model centered around the data collection activities of the Instrumentation System. The system receives signals and other data from remote sensors. The information is processed and stored on disk. Data cannot be lost. Trend calculations are performed as the signals and data are processed.

The system must keep up with the flow of incoming data. The hard deadline for data collection is equal to the period of the incoming data. The signal data must be available for viewing within 5 seconds, and be recorded on disk and available as trend information within 30 seconds.

div.head: Conceptual Structure
div.p: The conceptual structure is informally described in Figure 2. Signals and other data flow from the remote sensors through the Data Acquisition Connector to the Instrumentation System. The Data Acquisition Connector is a complex protocol that translates the incoming information to the internal message format. The information is then sent to the Data Manager where it is stored on disk for ondemand retrieval later. The information is also sent to the Trend Service which computes long-term trends for each remote sensor. The computed trend information is also stored on disk.

To describe the conceptual structure, we used a components and connectors model. Components are drawn as rounded boxes and the connectors (i.e., interfaces and protocols) are shown as lines or rectangles with square corners. We have found that lines tend to understate the importance and complexity of connectors. In our drawings, we have used rectangles to represent those connectors which have complex behavior (i.e., use complex protocols for communication).

Like components, connectors in the conceptual structure are also domain specific. For example, the conceptual structure has at least two different types of connectors. One type of connector, such as the connector from the remote sensors to the Data Manager carries a continuous stream of signal samples. The stream is produced at the rate of 150 samples per second. The other connector type conveys an event message. Such messages are sent only when necessary, (i.e., their traffic pattern is sporadic). One connector to the User Interface Manager is of this type and sends a message when an alarm occurs.

Typically, the product engineer would define the execution structure next, before applying any form of schedulability analysis. We used the conceptual structure as an application-level model for performing early analysis. The model showed that the system may be schedulable, but it has many assumptions that are more optimistic than warranted (since it does not take into account the overhead associated with the execution environment). If the application-level model was not schedulable, then we would have known that a major redesign of the system was needed [ 101.

The execution structure is important for performance estimation, scheduling analysis, sizing, and the initialization and termination of the computing environment. With the information available from the execution structure, we refined the execution times of the software components in our application-level model to include the time for: sending and receiving messages, writing data to the disk, bloclung, and the operating system overhead --_

div.head: Factor Alternatives
div.p: Although the requirements state that signals are sampled .it a rate of 150 times per second, the engineer can choose how often to send the data. The data could be sent as soon as a sample arrives or it could be buffered at different intervals. Here we looked at buffering 15 samples every 100 ms versus buffering 150 samples every second (1000 ms). Components in the conceptual structure can be grouped and assigned to tasks according to function or according to period. The function-driven model emphasizes functional cohesion, physical cohesion and minimum communication bandwidth required between tasks. The period-driven model considers an assignment guided by periodicity, that is, software components will be grouped by execution period. We can also determine the merits of having one task versus 16 tasks (one for each remote sensor) for the Data Acquisition Connector.

div.head: Experimental Results
div.p: We evaluated the design decisions in terms of their effects on system schedulability (i.e., all tasks complete before their respective deadlines). For those configurations that are schedulable, we computed the critical scaling factor. The critical scaling factor is the largest coefficient by which all execution times can be multiplied and still maintain a feasible schedule. It is one measure of excess processor time and how well the system accommodates the introduction of new tasks or an increase in the execution time of the existing tasks (a higher number being preferable).

We used this definition of schedulability and critical scaling factor to compare a variety of design decisions by lo00 ms 100 ms function-driven period-driven 1 task 16 tasks I Allocation I 1 task I 16 tasks I 1 task 1 16 tasks I To determine the importance of each of the factors, the results can be regressed on the three factors using a nonlinear regression model [3]. The resulting variation explains how much of the change of the critical scaling factor might be attributable to a change in the factors, individually, or in interaction with another factor. For example, the data buffering interval explained 48% of the variation individually and 6% when interacting with the assignment of function to tasks (Table 3). The data buffering interval and assignment of function to tasks had the greatest influence on schedulability. Table 2 shows that in most cases, the buffering interval of 100 ms was not schedulable. Since buffering has such a great influence on the schedulability (as determined in Table 3), the engineer may decide to perform a more detailed analysis of other intervals to determine which is optimal. The results also show that schedulability is improved when software components are grouped by period rather than by function. This checks with conventional intuitive real-time design practice which groups components by period. Using 16 tasks instead of one for the incurs additional costs from the operating system, increasing the overhead slightly. With this data in hand, the product engineer may decide that the gains in using a simpler design (with one task for each sensor) are worth the small amount of overhead incurred in the system.

div.head: Conclusions and Future Work
div.p: The experience from the experimental study suggests that working from architecture descriptions can help bridge the gap between physical systems and the representations that are required to apply real-time analysis techniques. The resulting analysis can also provide feedback to evaluate the design decisions made at the architecture level. The conceptual and execution structures separate the logical structure of the application from the concerns of the run-time environment. Mapping the conceptual structure to the execution structure explicitly records the design decisions that are often implicit when the structures are combined.

Real-time analysis need not be delayed until low-level design. The conceptual structure can provide insight into an application-level model that can be analyzed. Although such models are likely to include overly optimistic assumptions, early analysis can be beneficial in alerting the product engineer to potential problems that would require substantial redesign. It also can serve as a baseline system. As the system is refined, and an execution structure selected, additional details for the analysis can be added to the model. We can also use the baseline system to evaluate other design choices, using a variety of techniques for modifying the system and evaluating the system to see if it meets its realtime constraints.

In the initial system we described the data collection subsystem and developed a real-time analysis model in two stages, first looking at the application-level tasks, and then incorporating the overhead from the system platform. We have already extended the system to include the User Interface Manager and the Report Service to see the how system scales. In doing so, we are learning how to apply real-time analysis models to earlier stages in the design, and using the information obtained to make our representations for architecture more concrete. Our ultimate goal is to facilitate the evaluation and selection of alternative designs, and to verify the properties of the implemented system.
